title: Terminal Mastery & System Monitoring
summary: The terminal is where DevOps work happens. Mastering navigation, pipes and redirects, process monitoring, and performance tools is what separates someone who can use a Linux system from someone who can operate it.

sections.title: Shell navigation and essential commands
sections.body:
## The shell: your primary interface to Linux

The **shell** is a command interpreter — a program that reads commands you type, passes them to the operating system kernel for execution, and returns output to your screen. On modern Linux systems, the default shell is almost always **Bash** (Bourne Again SHell), though `zsh`, `fish`, and `dash` are also common. When you open a terminal, you're talking to a shell.

**Why the terminal matters for DevOps:** Graphical interfaces don't exist on servers. Kubernetes pods, CI runners, and cloud VMs are all text-only. Even when a GUI exists (like the AWS console), the command line is faster, scriptable, and auditable. Every meaningful DevOps operation — deploying code, debugging a crash, configuring a service, inspecting a container — eventually requires shell commands. The terminal is not a legacy interface; it's the control plane for modern infrastructure.

**How the shell processes a command:** When you type `ls -la /etc`, the shell:
1. Tokenizes the input into: command (`ls`), flags (`-la`), argument (`/etc`)
2. Expands any globs (`*.yaml`), variables (`$HOME`), or command substitutions (`` `date` `` or `$(date)`)
3. Forks a child process and uses `execve()` to replace it with the `ls` binary
4. Connects the child's stdout/stderr to your terminal
5. Waits for the child to finish and collects its exit code

**Pipes and redirection — the Unix philosophy:** Unix was built around the idea that programs should do one thing well and communicate through text streams. A **pipe** (`|`) connects the stdout of one program directly to the stdin of the next, creating a processing chain without writing temporary files. **Redirection** (`>`, `>>`, `2>`) sends streams to files. This composability — chaining `grep`, `awk`, `sort`, `uniq` — is far more powerful than any single monolithic tool.

**Exit codes:** Every command exits with a numeric status code. `0` means success. Non-zero means failure (the specific number varies by program). The shell exposes the last exit code in `$?`. Scripts use `set -euo pipefail` to exit immediately if any command fails, treating infrastructure automation as strictly as application code.

**Key navigation mental model:** The shell always has a **current working directory** (shown by `pwd`). Absolute paths start with `/` and work from anywhere. Relative paths are resolved from the current directory. `~` is shorthand for your home directory. `..` is the parent directory. `cd -` takes you back to wherever you just were — invaluable when you're jumping between directories.

```bash
# ── Navigation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pwd                     # print working directory
cd /var/log             # change to absolute path
cd ..                   # up one level
cd -                    # go back to last directory
cd ~                    # go to home directory

# ── Files and directories ────────────────────────────────────────────────
ls -la                  # long format, include hidden files
ls -lh                  # human-readable sizes
tree /etc | head -20    # visual directory tree

mkdir -p /tmp/work/sub  # create nested dirs
rm /tmp/test-file.txt 2>/dev/null || true  # cleanup example
rm -rf dir/             # delete directory (be very careful)
cp /workspace/config.yaml /tmp/config-copy.yaml  # copy
cp -r /workspace /tmp/workspace-copy         # copy directory
mv /tmp/config-copy.yaml /tmp/config-renamed.yaml  # rename or move

# ── Viewing files ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat /workspace/app.log  # print entire file
head -20 /workspace/app.log  # use 'less /workspace/app.log' interactively
head -20 /workspace/app.log  # first 20 lines
tail -20 /workspace/app.log  # last 20 lines
tail -f /var/log/dpkg.log &  # follow — new lines appear as they're written
sleep 1; kill %1 2>/dev/null
wc -l /workspace/app.log     # count lines

# ── Pipes and redirects ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# pipe: send stdout of left to stdin of right
ps aux | grep nginx
cat /etc/passwd | awk -F: '{print $1}' | sort

# redirect stdout to file (overwrite)
kubectl get pods -A > pods.txt

# redirect stdout to file (append)
echo "$(date): backup complete" >> /var/log/backup.log

# redirect stderr
command 2> error.log         # stderr to file
command > out.txt 2>&1       # both stdout and stderr to file
command &> all.log           # shorthand for both
command 2>/dev/null          # discard errors

# tee — write to file AND stdout simultaneously
kubectl apply -f /workspace/deployment.yaml | tee /tmp/apply.log

# ── Searching ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
find /etc -name '*.conf'                  # find by name
find /var/log -mtime -1 -name '*.log'     # modified in last 24h
grep -r 'error' /var/log --include='*.log' -l  # files containing 'error'
grep -n 'error' /workspace/app.log        # show line numbers
```

sections.title: Process and performance monitoring
sections.body:
## Why resource monitoring is a core DevOps skill

Production systems fail in predictable ways: CPU saturates and requests time out. Memory fills up and the OOM killer starts terminating processes. Disk fills up and applications can't write logs or state. Network becomes congested and latency spikes. Your job as a DevOps engineer is to detect these conditions before they cause an outage, diagnose the root cause when they do, and understand the signals well enough to set meaningful alerts.

**The four resources to watch:**

**CPU:** The processor executes instructions. **Load average** is the most important headline number — it measures how many processes are waiting to run (or waiting for I/O). A load average equal to the number of CPU cores means the system is fully busy but not overwhelmed. Above that, work is queuing. Below 0.7 × core count is typically healthy. High **%sy** (kernel/system CPU) often indicates excessive syscalls or context switching. High **%wa** (I/O wait) means the CPU is idle because it's waiting for disk.

**Memory:** Linux uses free RAM as disk cache (the **page cache**) to speed up reads. This is intentional, not waste. The `free -h` output shows a `buff/cache` column and an `available` column — the latter is what actually matters, as it includes memory the kernel can reclaim from cache on demand. When `available` approaches zero, the system starts **swapping** (writing RAM contents to disk), which causes severe performance degradation.

**Disk:** Two separate metrics matter: **space** (`df -h` — how much is used) and **I/O** (`iostat -x` — how fast data is moving). A disk can be 20% full but completely saturated with writes, causing slow I/O for everything. `%util` in `iostat` near 100% means the disk is a bottleneck, regardless of how much space is free. `await` measures the average time in milliseconds for an I/O request to complete — under 1ms for NVMe, 5–20ms for spinning disk is normal; significantly higher means saturation.

**Network:** `ss` (socket statistics) replaces the older `netstat` and is much faster on busy systems. It shows what processes are listening on which ports, and all active connections. In Kubernetes, network problems often manifest as pods unable to reach each other or the API server — `ss` and `curl` are your first debugging tools.

**The `/proc` filesystem:** Every piece of resource data ultimately comes from `/proc/`. `top`, `free`, `ps`, and `df` are all just readers of `/proc` that format the output nicely. Knowing how to read `/proc` directly gives you access to information that no high-level tool exposes, and works even when those tools aren't installed.

Knowing how to read system resource usage is essential for diagnosing performance issues and capacity planning.

```bash
# ── CPU and load ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
top                 # interactive: press M (memory sort), P (CPU sort), q (quit)
uptime              # load average: 1min, 5min, 15min
                    # load avg of 1.0 = 100% on a 1-core system
                    # load avg > CPU count = system is overloaded

# vmstat — virtual memory statistics
vmstat 1 5          # report every 1 second, 5 times
# Key columns: r (run queue), b (blocked), us (user CPU%), sy (system CPU%),
#              wa (iowait%), id (idle%)
# High wa% = disk I/O bottleneck

# mpstat — per-CPU stats (from sysstat package)
mpstat -P ALL 1 3

# ── Memory ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
free -h             # total, used, free, buffers/cache, available
# 'available' is what processes can actually use (includes reclaimable cache)

cat /proc/meminfo | grep -E 'MemTotal|MemFree|MemAvailable|Cached|Buffers'

# ── Disk ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
df -h               # disk space per filesystem
df -h /             # just root filesystem
du -sh /var/*       # disk usage per directory
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head -10  # top 10 largest log dirs

# iostat — disk I/O statistics (from sysstat)
iostat -x 1 3
# Key: %util (% time device was busy), await (avg wait time ms)
# %util near 100% = disk is saturated

# ── Network ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ss -tuln            # show listening TCP/UDP sockets
                    # -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening, -n numeric ports
ss -tp              # show TCP connections with process info
netstat -tuln       # older alternative to ss

# Network interface stats
ip -s link          # packet counters per interface
cat /proc/net/dev   # raw interface stats

# ── Per-process resource usage ───────────────────────────────────────────
# /proc/<pid>/ contains everything about a process
ls /proc/$$         # $$ = current shell PID
cat /proc/$$/status # memory, uid, state
cat /proc/$$/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '  # full command line

# open file descriptors and socket inspection
ls /proc/$$/fd | head -10           # open file descriptors for current process
ss -tlnp | grep :8000               # what's listening on port 8000
ss -tlnp                            # all listening TCP sockets
```

sections.title: Networking tools for debugging
sections.body:
## Debugging the network stack layer by layer

Networking problems in DevOps are almost always one of four things: **DNS doesn't resolve**, **the port isn't open**, **a firewall is blocking traffic**, or **the service is up but returning an error**. The tools in this section let you diagnose each layer independently, which is the only way to systematically eliminate possibilities.

**The practical network stack:** Although the full OSI 7-layer model is mostly theoretical, the stack you work with in practice has four relevant layers:
1. **Network/IP layer** — can packets reach the destination at all? (`ping`, `traceroute`)
2. **Transport/TCP layer** — is the port open and accepting connections? (`nc`, `ss`)
3. **DNS** — does the hostname resolve to the right IP? (`dig`, `nslookup`)
4. **Application layer** — is the service returning the right response? (`curl`)

**Start from DNS:** Most "I can't reach X" problems are actually DNS failures. `dig` is the authoritative DNS debugging tool — it shows you exactly which DNS server was queried, what the full response was, the TTL, and the query time. `+short` gives you just the IP when that's all you need. In Docker and Kubernetes, each container uses a custom DNS server (Docker's embedded DNS at `127.0.0.11`, Kubernetes' CoreDNS) — testing against those directly reveals whether a service discovery issue is DNS-related.

**Then test connectivity:** `ping` uses ICMP to test whether the destination is reachable at the IP layer. `traceroute` shows you every hop between you and the destination, revealing where packets are being dropped or delayed. `mtr` combines both into a live, continuously updating view — essential for diagnosing intermittent network issues.

**Then test the port:** `nc` (netcat) is the Swiss Army knife of network testing. `nc -zv host port` tests whether a TCP port is open without sending any application data. If `ping` succeeds but `nc` fails, the firewall or service binding is the problem. If DNS succeeds but `ping` fails, routing or firewall is the problem.

**Then test the application:** `curl` speaks HTTP (and HTTPS, FTP, and dozens of other protocols). It shows you exactly what the server responded with: status code, headers, body. The `-v` flag shows the full TLS handshake and HTTP exchange, which is invaluable for debugging authentication and TLS certificate problems. `-o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` gives you a clean one-line health check script.

**In Kubernetes:** Network debugging adds a layer because pod-to-pod traffic flows through the CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin. A service might be reachable from one pod but not another. `kubectl exec` lets you run network tools *inside* a pod to diagnose from its perspective.

These tools are used constantly to diagnose connectivity issues, inspect traffic, and test services.

```bash
# ── DNS resolution ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
dig google.com              # query DNS, shows full response
dig @127.0.0.11 google.com  # Docker internal DNS
dig google.com +short       # just the IP
nslookup google.com         # simpler alternative
host google.com             # simple forward lookup

# ── Connectivity ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8           # test reachability (ICMP)
traceroute 8.8.8.8          # trace route to host
mtr 8.8.8.8                 # traceroute + ping combined

# ── Port testing ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Is something listening on this port?
nc -zv k3s 6443             # k3s API port
nc -zuv 127.0.0.11 53      # Docker DNS (UDP)
telnet k3s 6443             # test k3s API

# ── HTTP testing with curl ────────────────────────────────────────────────
curl https://example.com                        # GET request
curl -I https://example.com                    # headers only (HEAD)
curl -v https://example.com                    # verbose: show full exchange
curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com  # just status code
```

```bash norun
# POST with JSON body (illustrative — requires a real API endpoint)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/data \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \
  -d '{"key": "value"}'
```

```bash
# ── In the sandbox — test k3s services ───────────────────────────────────
# The k3s API server is at https://k3s:6443
curl -k https://k3s:6443/healthz

# Test the FastAPI backend
curl http://localhost:8000/api/cluster/status
curl http://localhost:8000/api/lessons | python3 -m json.tool | head -20

# Test the ArgoCD UI (if port-forward is running)
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:80 &
sleep 2
curl -s http://localhost:8080/healthz
```

sections.title: Text processing: grep, awk, sed, cut
sections.body:
## Text as the universal interface

Linux configuration files are plain text. Log files are plain text. API responses, Kubernetes manifests, CI output, and shell command output are all plain text. The Unix philosophy treats text streams as the universal interface between tools — which means that mastering text processing tools is equivalent to mastering the data layer of your infrastructure.

**The core toolkit:**

**`grep`** searches for lines matching a pattern. At its simplest, it's a filter — you pipe data in and only matching lines come out. With `-r` it searches entire directory trees. With `-E` it accepts full regular expressions. With `-A`, `-B`, and `-C` it shows context lines around each match. In DevOps, `grep` is how you find errors in log files, locate config values, and search codebases.

**`awk`** processes structured text field by field. It reads input line by line, splits each line into fields by whitespace (or a custom delimiter with `-F`), and lets you apply conditions and transformations. The most common use case in DevOps is extracting specific columns from command output: `kubectl get pods | awk '{print $1, $3}'` prints only the pod name and status columns. `awk` also supports arithmetic, so you can sum a column of numbers (e.g., total CPU usage across all processes).

**`sed`** (stream editor) applies substitutions and transformations to text. `s/old/new/` replaces the first occurrence on each line; `s/old/new/g` replaces all. The `-i` flag edits files in-place. In DevOps automation, `sed` is commonly used to patch configuration files — changing a version number in a Kubernetes manifest, toggling a feature flag in a config file, or stripping comments from output.

**`cut`** extracts specific fields or character ranges. It's simpler than `awk` but faster for straightforward column extraction from delimited files.

**The pipeline pattern:** These tools become exponentially more powerful when chained with pipes. The classic log analysis pipeline is: `cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10` — extract IP addresses, sort them, count duplicates, sort by frequency, show the top 10. This idiom — extract, sort, deduplicate/aggregate, rank — applies to almost any text analysis task you'll encounter.

**Regular expressions:** Both `grep -E` and `sed` accept POSIX extended regular expressions. Knowing the basics — `.` (any char), `*` (zero or more), `+` (one or more), `[]` (character class), `^` (start of line), `$` (end of line), `|` (alternation) — dramatically increases what you can filter and extract.

DevOps lives in log files, config files, and command output. These tools let you extract exactly what you need.

```bash
# ── grep — find matching lines ────────────────────────────────────────────
grep 'ERROR' app.log
grep -i 'error' app.log              # case-insensitive
grep -v '^#' /etc/hosts              # invert: lines NOT starting with #
grep -E '(ERROR|WARN|FATAL)' app.log # extended regex
grep -n 'Restart' app.log            # show line numbers
grep -c 'ERROR' app.log              # count matching lines
grep -rn 'password' /etc/ 2>/dev/null # recursive search
grep -A 3 'EXCEPTION' app.log        # 3 lines after each match

# ── awk — column-based processing ────────────────────────────────────────
# Fields: $1=first, $2=second, $NF=last, NR=line number
kubectl get pods | awk '{print $1, $3}'        # name and status columns
kubectl get pods | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}'       # skip header line
df -h | awk 'NR>1 && $5+0 > 80 {print $0}'    # disks > 80% full

# Calculation
ps aux | awk 'NR>1 {sum += $3} END {print "Total CPU%:", sum}'

# Custom delimiter
cat /etc/passwd | awk -F: '{print $1 ":" $7}'  # user:shell

# ── sed — stream substitution ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Replace
echo 'image: nginx:latest' | sed 's/latest/1.25/'
sed -i 's/replicas: 1/replicas: 3/' deployment.yaml

# Delete lines
sed '/^#/d' config.yaml              # remove comment lines
sed '/^$/d' config.yaml              # remove blank lines

# In-place edit with backup
sed -i.bak 's/log_level: info/log_level: debug/' /workspace/config.yaml && mv /workspace/config.yaml.bak /workspace/config.yaml

# ── cut — extract columns ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd              # field 1, delimiter :  (usernames)
kubectl get pods | cut -c1-40        # first 40 characters

# ── sort, uniq, wc ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
# ↑ top 10 IPs by request count

wc -l app.log              # count lines
wc -c app.log              # count bytes
```

sections.title: Exercise: system health report script
sections.body:
## Building a real operational tool

System health scripts are a practical staple of DevOps work. Before you have a full observability stack (Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog), a shell script that snapshots key metrics is often the first thing you write when you take responsibility for a new server or cluster. Even with a full observability stack, having a quick one-command health dump is invaluable during incidents.

This exercise asks you to synthesize everything from this week — navigation, process monitoring, disk/memory inspection, network socket listing, and cross-service connectivity testing — into a single coherent script.

**Design principles for operational scripts:**
- `set -euo pipefail` at the top: `-e` exits on any error, `-u` treats unset variables as errors, `-o pipefail` catches failures inside pipes. Together they make scripts fail loudly rather than silently producing wrong output.
- Use clear section headers and consistent formatting so the output is scannable at a glance during an incident.
- Include a timestamp so you know when the snapshot was taken.
- Test external dependencies (like `curl k3s:6443/healthz`) and show a clear PASS/FAIL, not just the raw output.
- Keep it idempotent — running it twice should produce the same result and leave no side effects.

**What a good health report tells you immediately:**
- Is the system under load? (uptime / load average)
- Is memory tight? (`free -h` available column)
- Is disk about to fill up? (`df -h` usage percentages)
- Is there a runaway process? (`ps` sorted by CPU or memory)
- Are the expected services listening? (`ss -tuln`)
- Can we reach the control plane? (`curl k3s healthz`)
- How many workloads are actually running? (`kubectl` pod count)

Write a `system-health.sh` script that produces a snapshot report of the sandbox environment.

**Requirements:**
1. Print OS version and kernel
2. Show uptime and load average
3. Show memory usage (used / total)
4. Show disk usage for `/` and `/data`
5. List the top 5 processes by memory
6. Show all listening TCP ports
7. Check if the k3s API is reachable (`curl -k https://k3s:6443/healthz`)
8. Show number of running pods in each namespace

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

HR='────────────────────────────────'

echo "=== System Health Report ==="
echo "Generated: $(date)"
echo ""

echo "── OS & Kernel ──"
# TODO: print OS info and kernel version

echo ""
echo "── Load & Uptime ──"
# TODO: show uptime output

echo ""
echo "── Memory ──"
# TODO: show free -h output

echo ""
echo "── Disk ──"
# TODO: show df -h for / and /data

echo ""
echo "── Top 5 Processes by Memory ──"
# TODO: ps aux sorted by %MEM, top 5

echo ""
echo "── Listening Ports ──"
# TODO: ss -tuln

echo ""
echo "── k3s API ──"
# TODO: curl -k -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://k3s:6443/healthz

echo ""
echo "── Pod Count by Namespace ──"
# TODO: kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c
```

**Try it:**

```bash
# Write your script to /workspace/system-health.sh, then run it:
# (open the file in the editor panel, or use the terminal directly)
chmod +x /workspace/system-health.sh 2>/dev/null && /workspace/system-health.sh || echo "Create system-health.sh first by editing the template above"
```
